items.label: A
items.critique: Secret bookcase passage, 'at whatever the cost!', 'Unsavory elements dwell in the shadows!', 'Good luck, Apprentice!' and an imperative journal: the Nox wizard chapter's voice, typo-level apostrophe included.

items.label: B
items.critique: 'Greetings, Adept!', 'dire need', 'foul demoness', '...sooner than you think' - breathless exclamatory plot-pushing typical of Westwood.

items.label: C
items.critique: A careful institutional backstory (Reeve's grant, a month's deadline), precise physical description ('the size of a cup's mouth', 'my father's thumb worn into the edge') and a long journal: thoughtful, but not Nox.

items.label: D
items.critique: Political intrigue (the moot, the charter), a crow's-foot token, and the stately 'the office of Reeve is not ungrateful' - a different, more literary writer.

items.label: E
items.critique: Fragmentary grief ('That's it. That's his mark. ...Forgive me.') and three-generation detail are affecting, but the restraint and colon-led lists are not Westwood's register.

items.label: F
items.critique: 'kind sir!', breathless short pleading, 'Could you... would you', a one-line thanks and a 'Retrieve X from Y near Z' journal: unmistakably Nox's townsfolk side quest.

items.label: G
items.critique: A drowned-souls ledger, 'I'll write the carter's name in it tonight; he has earned his place' - elegiac, semicolon-rich, and far too composed for Nox.

items.label: H
items.critique: 'Gahhhhhh! No! Don't kill me!', the half-blind hermit, and a reward scroll about bats: Nox's broad slapstick humour exactly.

items.label: I
items.critique: Inn named for a lantern fished from the water, 'lighting their dice', 'There she is' - charming, but its wistful texture and narrative journal give it away.

items.label: J
items.critique: 'valiant [Class]', 'nettlesome urchins', explicit directions ('East of here', 'center of town') and a 'buy supplies, then see the Captain' handoff are classic Westwood tutorial-town writing.

tells: Journal form: Westwood uses one imperative clause ('Retrieve the [Thing].'); the new texts write two or three past-tense sentences naming who asked, what it is, its history and where it is.
Object description: the new texts lavish sensory detail on the heirloom (metal, size, marks, wear) and its lineage; Westwood names the object and moves on.
Emotion: Westwood's speakers are loud (exclamations, 'Gahhhhhh!', 'kind sir!', 'Please hurry'); the new ones are restrained, elegiac, with ellipsis-pauses and understatement.
Reminder lines: Westwood repeats the urgency or a warning; the new reminders give a precise location plus a characterful aside.

Rewards and humour: Westwood's rewards are campaign-relevant (spells, scrolls, next destination) and its humour broad and slapstick; the new ones offer a found item plus 'a bed/flour/potions for life' and lean on dry wit.
Repetition across new texts: the same shared map furniture (Reeve, ford, watchtower, barrow, mill) and the same 'Will you...?' closing question on every offer.
